consensus_summary: Iron symbolizes strength, hardness, and unyielding/crushing power, expressed chiefly in the messianic 'rod of iron' (Ps 2:9; Rev 2:27; 12:5; 19:15) and Daniel's iron fourth kingdom (Dan 2:40), with secondary senses of oppression (iron furnace/yoke), stubbornness, sharpening, and military might. The fourth-kingdom-as-Rome reading appears explicitly as a common alternative in Response A.
book_summary: Iron is the crushing strength of Daniel's fourth kingdom, identified historically as Rome — the empire ruling when Christ came (Dan 2:40; 8:20-21).
consensus_core_identification: Iron = strength/hardness/irresistible, crushing power, applied broadly to messianic rule, oppressive empires, and other contexts.
book_core_identification: Iron = the crushing strength of Daniel's fourth kingdom, specifically Rome.
boundary_disagreement: The book fixes iron's symbolic referent to one case — Daniel's fourth kingdom (Rome) — thereby excluding or leaving aside the rod-of-iron messianic rule texts (Psalm 2; Revelation), the iron furnace/yoke of oppression, iron-sharpens-iron, stubbornness, and other consensus applications. The consensus treats the fourth kingdom as one prominent instance of a broader strength/crushing-power symbol; the book makes it the definition.
material_contradiction: None. The book's identification (crushing strength of the fourth kingdom = Rome) is explicitly listed as a common alternative in Response A and is grounded in the same Daniel 2:40 text all responses cite; it does not deny that iron elsewhere signifies strength or rule.
rationale: Both readings share the same underlying quality — crushing, subduing strength drawn from Daniel 2:40. The consensus generalizes this into a multivalent symbol with the messianic rod of iron as its most prominent expression; the book narrows the symbol to a single historical-prophetic referent, Rome as Daniel's fourth kingdom. Since the central category (iron as crushing imperial strength in Daniel's vision) is preserved and even named by the consensus, this is a material narrowing of extension rather than a replaced referent, so REFINED rather than DIVERGENT or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH, since Response A lists 'the fourth world empire (traditionally identified as Rome)' as a common alternative with the very same basis texts, making the book's entry simply a selection among recognized consensus meanings rather than a real boundary change. The counter is that the book presents this as the meaning of iron, implicitly displacing the rod-of-iron primary sense, which is a genuine narrowing of the term's extension. On citations: Dan 2:40 strongly supports crushing strength of the fourth kingdom, but neither printed verse names Rome; Dan 8:20-21 only identifies Media-Persia and Greece, leaving the Rome identification inferential (sequence plus 'the empire when Christ came'), hence only partial support.
